title: Convolutional networks
lead: The convolutional network built from the operation up: a convolution computed by hand and in code, the cost of every layer counted, the residual connection that made depth trainable, and the same machinery used to detect objects, to segment images and volumes into measured surfaces, and to check what a classifier is actually looking at.
prerequisites: Module 01: the supervised learning set-up, cross-entropy from maximum likelihood, train, validation and test splits with leakage, and the bias–variance decomposition.
Module 02: MLPs, backpropagation in matrix form, He initialisation, Adam and AdamW with learning-rate schedules, batch and layer normalisation, and the overfit-one-batch debugging habit.
Linear algebra: matrix–vector products, transposes, and sparse and banded matrices.
Calculus: partial derivatives and the chain rule over indexed sums.
Python: NumPy slicing and broadcasting, a PyTorch `nn.Module`, and the training loop of Module 02, Section 13.
outcomes: Compute a 2D convolution (in deep learning, a cross-correlation) by hand on a small image, implement it in NumPy with explicit loops and with im2col, and match `torch.nn.functional.conv2d` to floating-point round-off.

Derive the output size $\lfloor (H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1)/s \rfloor + 1$ for any padding, stride and dilation, compute a network's receptive field layer by layer, and explain why the effective receptive field is smaller.
Count the parameters, multiply-accumulates, FLOPs and activation memory of a standard, $1 \times 1$, grouped or depthwise-separable convolution, and say which convention a paper's "FLOPs" follow.
Derive why identity shortcuts keep the gradient alive in a deep network, and reproduce the degradation of a 55-layer plain network and its residual fix.

Name the one idea that each of LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, Inception, ResNet, DenseNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet and ConvNeXt contributed, check their headline parameter counts, and place the vision transformer relative to them.

Choose label-preserving augmentations, a normalisation suited to the batch size and a transfer strategy (which layers to keep, linear probe or fine-tuning) for a small dataset, and justify each choice with measurements.
Compute IoU, non-maximum suppression and average precision by hand, and explain anchors, the focal loss and the difference between one-stage and two-stage detectors.
Train a U-Net, evaluate it with Dice and IoU ($D = 2J/(1 + J)$), and turn a predicted mask into area, perimeter, volume and surface-area measurements whose biases you can state.
Compute Grad-CAM from its definition, use it to expose a classifier that relies on a spurious cue, and state what such maps cannot show.
Estimate the parameter, compute and memory cost of 1D and 3D convolutional networks, including why 3D models train on patches with group normalisation.
software: PyTorch 2.x; the CPU build is enough.
scikit-learn, for `load_digits` and `train_test_split`; nothing is downloaded.
matplotlib, with `contourpy` (installed with it) for marching squares.
Optional: scikit-image, for the marching-cubes step of Exercise 14.
Optional, for a Lab 4 extension that is shown but not executed: `torchvision` and a 44.7 MB download of ResNet-18 weights.
Optional, for a Lab 3 extension that is shown but not executed: the CIFAR-10 dataset (about 170 MB, through `torchvision`) and a free GPU on Google Colab.

sections.title: Images are not vectors
sections.purpose: Show why a dense network is the wrong architecture for images and derive the convolution layer from two assumptions, locality and stationarity, with the parameter counts that make the case.
must_cover: The count from the source: a 224x224 colour image is 224*224*3 = 150,528 numbers; a dense first layer of 1,000 units has 150,528*1,000 + 1,000 = 150,529,000 parameters (602,116,000 bytes in float32, 574 MiB), and it must learn separately that an edge at the top left and the same edge at the bottom right are the same thing.
Locality: a pixel's meaning depends far more on its neighbours than on distant pixels; support it with the measured correlation-versus-distance numbers on load_digits (worked example).
Stationarity: the statistics of small patches are the same everywhere in the image, so a detector useful at one position is useful at every position; this licenses weight sharing.

The progression at a fixed output of 224x224x64 from a 224x224x3 input with 3x3 windows: dense layer 150,528 x 3,211,264 = 4.83e11 weights; locally connected (each output unit sees its own 3x3x3 window with its own 27 weights) 3,211,264 x 27 = 86,704,128 weights; convolution (the 27 weights shared across positions, one set per output channel) 64*27 + 64 = 1,792 parameters. Locality removes the first factor; weight sharing divides by the 50,176 positions. The parameter count of a convolution no longer depends on the image size.

Statistical strength: every shared weight receives a gradient contribution from all 50,176 positions of every training image, so one image informs a filter as much as tens of thousands of examples would inform an untied weight.

Definitions written out: a translation T_tau shifts an image by tau = (tau1, tau2); f is equivariant if f(T_tau x) = T_tau f(x) and invariant if f(T_tau x) = f(x). Convolution is equivariant (proved in s2); pooling and global averaging give approximate invariance (s5). Classification wants invariance; segmentation and detection want equivariance.

The inductive-bias trade: a convolution is a dense layer whose matrix is constrained to be sparse and weight-tied, so it represents fewer functions; that is the point, because the functions it drops are ones images do not need. Preview Lab 2: shuffling the pixel order with one fixed permutation leaves an MLP's accuracy unchanged and hurts a CNN.
Where the assumptions hold and where they do not: grids with local, stationary statistics (images, signals, volumes, spectra; s13) benefit; tabular rows, whose column order is arbitrary, do not.
worked_examples: Dense first layer on a 224x224x3 image with 1,000 hidden units: 150,528 x 1,000 + 1,000 = 150,529,000 parameters; at 4 bytes each, 602,116,000 bytes (574 MiB, or 602 MB in decimal units) for one layer.

Dense -> locally connected -> convolutional, output 224x224x64, 3x3 windows: 4.83e11 -> 86,704,128 -> 1,792 parameters; the ratio of locally connected weights to shared weights, 86,704,128 / 1,728 = 50,176, is exactly the number of output positions.

Locality measured on scikit-learn's digits (1,797 images of 8x8 pixels; pixels whose standard deviation exceeds 0.5 on the 0-16 scale): mean correlation between pixels at distance 1 is +0.42, at sqrt(2) +0.17, at 2 -0.04, at 2-3 -0.06, beyond 3 about -0.04. Neighbours carry information about each other; pixels two or more apart carry almost none. Include the ten-line NumPy snippet (np.corrcoef over pixel columns, pairs binned by Euclidean distance) so the reader can redo it.

'Locally connected': lines from a 3x3 window only, with a second unit at another position whose 9 lines carry different labels (w1..w9 versus v1..v9). 'Convolutional': the same two windows, both labelled w1..w9. Caption gives the counts for 224x224x3 -> 224x224x64: 4.83e11, 86.7 million, 1,792.

checks: A layer maps a 32x32x3 image to 32x32x16 with 5x5 windows. How many parameters as a convolution with biases, and how many weights as a locally connected layer? -> Convolution 16*5*5*3 + 16 = 1,216; locally connected 32*32*16 = 16,384 output units x 75 weights = 1,228,800 (plus 16,384 biases).

Should a classifier that answers 'is there a crack in this image?' be equivariant or invariant to shifts? And a network that segments the crack? -> The classifier should be invariant (the label does not move); the segmentation network should be equivariant (the mask moves with the image).

sections.title: The convolution operation
sections.purpose: Define the operation exactly, compute it by hand, prove its translation equivariance, and write it as a matrix so that its backward pass and the transposed convolution follow.
must_cover: The single-channel definition with bias, indices from 0 and the output index at the window's top-left corner: Y_{i,j} = b + sum_{u=0}^{k-1} sum_{v=0}^{k-1} K_{u,v} X_{i+u, j+v} (the source's equation).

Cross-correlation versus convolution: the mathematical convolution (K * X)_{i,j} = sum K_{u,v} X_{i-u, j-v} flips the kernel; the two differ only by K_{u,v} -> K_{k-1-u, k-1-v}. Because K is learned, the flipped kernel is learned instead and nothing is lost; every framework computes cross-correlation and calls it convolution. Consequences: scipy.signal.convolve2d does not match torch.nn.functional.conv2d unless the kernel is flipped (Lab 1 checks it); symmetric kernels (blur) give identical results; antisymmetric ones (Sobel, [1, 0, -1]) differ by a sign.

Hand-designed kernels and the sum-of-weights rule: box blur (all 1/9, sum 1, preserves flat regions), Gaussian blur (1/16)[[1,2,1],[2,4,2],[1,2,1]] (sum 1), sharpen [[0,-1,0],[-1,5,-1],[0,-1,0]] (sum 1: identity minus a Laplacian), Sobel-x [[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]] (sum 0: zero on flat regions, responds to horizontal change, i.e. vertical edges), Laplacian [[0,1,0],[1,-4,1],[0,1,0]] (sum 0). Learned first-layer filters look like these (s14 shows Lab 2's).

Equivariance proved in two lines: with (T_tau X)_{i,j} = X_{i-tau1, j-tau2}, (K star T_tau X)_{i,j} = sum K_{u,v} X_{i+u-tau1, j+v-tau2} = (K star X)_{i-tau1, j-tau2} = (T_tau (K star X))_{i,j}. It holds exactly on an infinite grid or with circular padding, and away from the borders with zero padding (Lab 1 measures both).

The convolution as a matrix: in 1D a length-5 input and the kernel (1, 2, 3) give the 3x5 banded (Toeplitz) matrix with rows (1,2,3,0,0), (0,1,2,3,0), (0,0,1,2,3); in 2D a doubly block-Toeplitz matrix. A convolution layer is a dense layer whose matrix has k^2 nonzeros per row and tied values.

The backward pass follows from the matrix form: if y = Mx then dL/dx = M^T dL/dy, and applying M^T is a 'full' convolution with the kernel, the transposed convolution (named here, used for upsampling in s12). The weight gradient dL/dK_{u,v} = sum_{i,j} dL/dY_{i,j} X_{i+u, j+v} is a cross-correlation of the input with the output gradient. A convolution's backward pass is two more convolutions, about twice the forward cost (the argument of Module 02, Section 3).
Borders previewed: without padding a k x k kernel gives H - k + 1 outputs per axis; padding modes follow in s3.
worked_examples: The same X with the Gaussian blur gives [[1.125,1.6875,1.875],[1.25,1.75,1.8125],[1.5,1.5625,1.375]] (values pulled toward the local mean); with the sharpen kernel [[0,11,1],[-7,-4,17],[11,5,-9]].

Matrix form in 1D: kernel (1,2,3), x = (1,0,2,1,3): Mx = (7,7,13), identical to np.correlate(x, w, 'valid'). Backward: for an output gradient g = (1,-1,2), M^T g = (1,1,3,1,6), identical to np.convolve(g, w, 'full'): the transposed convolution.

Gallery: the 12x12 'letter F' test image used by the widget and its responses to box blur, sharpen, Sobel-x, Sobel-y and Laplacian, on a diverging colour map centred at zero; each panel labelled with its kernel and the sum of its weights.

checks: Why does F.conv2d match scipy.signal.correlate2d but not scipy.signal.convolve2d? -> Frameworks compute cross-correlation; convolve2d flips the kernel. Flip it (K[::-1, ::-1]) and they agree.
A kernel's weights sum to zero. What does it output on a constant image, away from the borders? -> Zero, since sum K_{u,v} c = c sum K_{u,v} = 0: such kernels respond only to change.
For an input of length 6 and a 3-tap kernel without padding, what is the shape of M and how many entries can be nonzero? -> 4x6, with 12 nonzeros (three per row).

sections.title: Output size, padding, stride, dilation and the receptive field
sections.purpose: Derive the shape arithmetic every architecture diagram relies on, and compute how far each output unit can see.
must_cover: Derive the output size by counting window positions along one axis: after padding there are H + 2p positions; a kernel of size k with dilation d spans d(k-1) + 1 of them; valid start positions are 0, s, 2s, ... up to H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1; so H_out = floor((H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1)/s) + 1, which reduces to the source's floor((H + 2p - k)/s) + 1 at d = 1.
'Same' padding: s = 1 and p = d(k-1)/2 keep H_out = H; it needs d(k-1) even, so odd kernels; an even kernel cannot be padded symmetrically (PyTorch's padding='same' then pads one side more).
Stride 2 with k = 3 and p = 1 maps an even H to H/2 (floor((H-1)/2) + 1 = H/2) and an odd H to (H+1)/2: 'stride 2 halves it' (source), with the odd case stated.
The floor discards input silently: H = 11, k = 3, p = 0, s = 3 gives 3 outputs that read columns 0-8; columns 9 and 10 are never read and no framework warns.
Padding modes: zero (the default), reflect, replicate, circular. Zero padding lets the network detect the border, which leaks absolute position into an otherwise equivariant layer.
Dilation: the kernel samples every d-th input; parameters are unchanged while the span grows to d(k-1) + 1.

The receptive field: the set of input positions that can influence one output unit. Derive the recurrence with the jump Delta_l (the distance, in input pixels, between adjacent units of layer l): r_0 = 1, Delta_0 = 1; r_l = r_{l-1} + (k_l - 1) d_l Delta_{l-1}; Delta_l = Delta_{l-1} s_l. Pooling layers enter with their window and stride.

Stacked small kernels (source: VGG's whole insight): n stacked 3x3 stride-1 layers have r = 2n + 1, so two 3x3 layers see what one 5x5 sees with 18C^2 instead of 25C^2 weights (28% fewer) and three see what one 7x7 sees with 27C^2 instead of 49C^2 (45% fewer), with a nonlinearity between each.

Downsampling multiplies the jump: after one stride-2 layer every 3x3 adds 4 pixels instead of 2 (source: strides and pooling grow the field faster). Dilated stacks grow exponentially: 3x3 layers with d = 1, 2, 4, 8 reach 31; dilations sharing a common factor leave gaps (gridding).

The theoretical receptive field is an upper bound. The effective receptive field (Luo et al. 2016), where the gradient of an output actually lands, is roughly Gaussian and much smaller: for SmallResNet's last stage (theoretical 49x49), Lab 3 measures about 44% of the input-gradient mass inside the central 9x9 and 89% inside 25x25.

Why it matters: a network whose effective receptive field is smaller than the object classifies texture rather than shape (source failure mode; Geirhos et al. 2019 measured a texture bias in ImageNet CNNs). Compute it; the recurrence makes this a five-minute task.
worked_examples: Output sizes for H = 11, k = 3 and (p, s, d) = (0,1,1) -> 9; (1,1,1) -> 11; (1,2,1) -> 6; (0,2,1) -> 5; (2,1,2) -> 11; (0,1,2) -> 7; (0,3,1) -> 3, reading columns 0-8 only. These seven are the configurations Lab 1 checks against PyTorch.

ResNet's stem on 224x224: a 7x7 convolution with stride 2 and padding 3 gives floor((224 + 6 - 7)/2) + 1 = 112; a 3x3 max pool with stride 2 and padding 1 gives floor((112 + 2 - 3)/2) + 1 = 56. Its receptive field: 7 after the convolution (jump 2), 7 + 2*2 = 11 after the pool (jump 4).

VGG-16's receptive field layer by layer: conv1_1 3, conv1_2 5, pool1 6 (jump 2), conv2_1 10, conv2_2 14, pool2 16 (jump 4), conv3_1 24, conv3_2 32, conv3_3 40, pool3 44 (jump 8), conv4_1 60, conv4_2 76, conv4_3 92, pool4 100 (jump 16), conv5_1 132, conv5_2 164, conv5_3 196, pool5 212 (jump 32).
Dilated 3x3 stack with d = 1, 2, 4, 8: r = 3, 7, 15, 31 in four layers; an undilated stack needs 15 layers to reach 31.

sections.title: Channels, parameters and FLOPs
sections.purpose: Generalise to many channels, write the layer as one matrix multiply, and count parameters, multiply-accumulates, FLOPs and memory so that any architecture table can be checked.
must_cover: The multi-channel equation (source): Y_{c,i,j} = b_c + sum_{c'=1}^{C_in} sum_{u,v} K_{c,c',u,v} X_{c', i+u, j+v}; the weight tensor has shape (C_out, C_in, k, k) and activations (B, C, H, W) in PyTorch (TensorFlow defaults to channels-last).
Each output channel is one filter spanning all input channels; a feature map is one output channel; a layer is C_out filters.

im2col: unfold every k x k x C_in window into a column of length C_in k^2, giving a (C_in k^2) x (H_out W_out) matrix; the layer is then one matrix multiply (C_out x C_in k^2)(C_in k^2 x H_out W_out). This is how CPU libraries and many GPU kernels compute convolutions (FFT and Winograd methods exist; name them only). The cost: each input value is copied up to k^2 times (9x memory for 3x3 at stride 1).

Counting: parameters k^2 C_in C_out + C_out; multiply-accumulates (MACs) k^2 C_in C_out H_out W_out; FLOPs = 2 x MACs (one multiply and one add each: the counting behind the 2N FLOPs per forward pass of Module 02, Section 2). ResNet, EfficientNet and ConvNeXt report multiply-adds and call them FLOPs (MobileNet calls them Mult-Adds): check the convention before comparing.

Conventions, stated once for the module: counts are MACs, and FLOPs = 2 x MACs, with bias additions and activations left out unless stated; memory computed from tensor sizes is in binary units (1 MiB = 2^20 bytes, 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes) and download sizes are decimal MB as published, so where the two forms differ both are given once (s1: 574 MiB, 602 MB). The series' FLOP convention for transformers is Module 06's (Module 06, Section 11); nothing in this module needs it.

Where parameters and compute live (source: parameters are cheap in convolutions; compute is spent on the spatial extent): parameters do not depend on H and W; compute is proportional to H_out W_out. Early high-resolution layers dominate compute; late wide layers and dense heads dominate parameters (VGG-16 numbers).
Activation memory: an output of shape (C, H, W) in float32 takes 4CHW bytes per image, and training keeps it for the backward pass (Module 02: training memory scales with depth times batch).
Backward cost: the input gradient and the weight gradient are each a convolution of the same size as the forward one (s2), so a training step costs about 3x the forward FLOPs.
Bias and normalisation: with batch normalisation directly after a convolution the bias is redundant (BN subtracts the mean), hence bias=False in the source's code.
worked_examples: The source's layer: 3x3, 64 -> 128 channels, 56x56 output. Parameters 3*3*64*128 + 128 = 73,728 + 128 = 73,856. MACs 73,728 x 3,136 = 231,211,008. FLOPs 2 x 231,211,008 = 462,422,016, about 462 million; adding the 128 x 3,136 = 401,408 bias additions gives 462,823,424, the source's '463 MFLOPs'. State the convention with every count.
The same layer by im2col: the column matrix has 576 x 3,136 = 1,806,336 entries (7,225,344 bytes, 6.9 MiB, in float32), 9.0 times the 200,704-entry input; the multiply is (128 x 576)(576 x 3,136).
Activation memory of that layer's output: 128 x 56 x 56 x 4 = 1,605,632 bytes, 1.53 MiB per image, and 392 MiB (411 MB) for a batch of 256.

VGG-16 at 224x224, counted from its layer list with a short script: 138,357,544 parameters, of which 123,642,856 (89%) are in the three dense layers; 15.35 G multiply-adds in the convolutions against 0.12 G in the dense layers (0.8%).
ResNet-18 at 224x224, counted the same way: 11,689,512 parameters and 1.81 G multiply-adds; the paper's Table 1 reports '1.8 x 10^9 FLOPs', so its 'FLOPs' are multiply-adds.

sections.title: Pooling, downsampling and invariance
sections.purpose: Explain how networks reduce resolution, why that buys only approximate translation invariance, and how global average pooling lets a network take any input size.
must_cover: Max pooling, 2x2 with stride 2 (source): halves H and W, keeps the strongest response, has no parameters; its backward pass routes each window's gradient entirely to the position that held the maximum.

Average pooling; global average pooling (GAP) collapses each channel's map to one number, C x H x W -> C, replacing the giant dense layers of early networks and letting the network accept any input size (source). Compare VGG-16's fc6 (25,088 x 4,096 + 4,096 = 102,764,544 parameters) with a GAP head of 512 x 1,000 + 1,000 = 513,000.

Strided convolution as learned downsampling (source: modern networks often downsample with a strided convolution, letting the layer learn what to keep): ResNet's stage transitions, ConvNeXt's separate downsampling layers.

Invariance is approximate: a stride-2 operation is equivariant only to shifts by multiples of 2, and a one-pixel shift can change every pooled value (worked example). Subsampling without low-pass filtering aliases, as in signal processing; Zhang (2019) blurs before subsampling ('anti-aliased' pooling) and reports more shift-stable outputs; Azulay and Weiss (2019) document predictions changing under one-pixel shifts.

Measured in Lab 2: on 8x8 digits a CNN with two 2x2 max pools and a flatten-dense head drops from about 98.4% to 67% accuracy when test images move one pixel to the right (the MLP drops to 42%); on digits placed at random on a 16x16 canvas, the CNN with GAP reaches about 93% and the same convolutions with a flatten head about 89%. Equivariant layers do not make an invariant classifier; the head and the training data decide.

Why downsample: each 2x reduction cuts the FLOPs of later layers by 4; it doubles the jump and so speeds receptive-field growth; and the convention of halving H and W while doubling C keeps per-layer compute roughly constant across stages.
worked_examples: Max pooling X = [[1,3,2,0],[4,2,1,1],[0,1,5,2],[2,2,3,4]] gives [[4,2],[2,5]]. Shift the input one column left (drop the first column, append zeros): [[3,2,0,0],[2,1,1,0],[1,5,2,0],[2,3,4,0]] pools to [[3,1],[5,4]] - every output changes. Shift by two columns: [[2,0],[5,0]], the original right column moved one cell left.
GAP head versus VGG-16's flatten head: 513,000 parameters against 102,764,544 for fc6 alone.

SmallResNet on 32x32 (Lab 3): the second convolution of every stage costs 9,437,184 multiply-adds (9*32*32*32*32 = 9*64*64*16*16 = 9*128*128*8*8 = 9*256*256*4*4) - halving H and W while doubling C keeps it constant.

Two classifier heads compared: flatten + dense (C*H*W inputs, position-specific weights; VGG-16's 7x7x512 = 25,088 -> 4,096, 102.8 M parameters) versus global average pooling + dense (C inputs; 512 -> 1,000, 0.5 M).

A GAP network trained on 32x32 images is given 48x48 ones. Does it run, and can you trust the answer? -> It runs (GAP returns C numbers at any size), but objects now sit at a different scale relative to the receptive fields, so test before trusting.

sections.title: Cheaper convolutions: 1x1, grouped and depthwise-separable
sections.purpose: Show how to mix channels cheaply and how to factorise a convolution, with the cost saving derived, because every efficient architecture in s7-s9 is built from these pieces.
must_cover: 1x1 convolution (source): Y_{c,i,j} = b_c + sum_{c'} W_{c,c'} X_{c',i,j}, a dense layer applied independently at every pixel; C_in C_out + C_out parameters; changes the channel count and adds a per-pixel nonlinearity (Lin et al. 2014, Network in Network).

Bottlenecks (source: Inception and later designs): reduce channels with a 1x1 before an expensive k x k and expand after; the cost of a k x k convolution at fixed resolution scales with C_in C_out, so reducing both sides by r divides it by r^2.
Grouped convolution (AlexNet's two-GPU split; ResNeXt): the C_in channels are split into g groups, each convolved only with its own C_out/g filters: k^2 C_in C_out / g parameters.
Depthwise convolution: g = C_in = C_out, one k x k filter per channel, k^2 C parameters.

Depthwise-separable convolution (source): depthwise k x k followed by pointwise 1x1. Derive per output position: standard k^2 C_in C_out MACs; separable k^2 C_in + C_in C_out; ratio 1/C_out + 1/k^2, about 1/9 for 3x3 kernels on wide layers (the source's 'a factor of roughly k^2').

What is given up: each output channel's spatial filter becomes a combination of C_in fixed per-channel spatial filters, a restricted family. MobileNet's Table 4 puts the price at about one point of ImageNet accuracy for about 8.5x less compute (70.6% with 569 M multiply-adds and 4.2 M parameters, against 71.7%, 4,866 M and 29.3 M with full convolutions).
FLOPs are not run time: depthwise layers do few operations per byte moved, so on GPUs they often run well below peak and the speed-up is smaller than the FLOP ratio. Measure on the target hardware.
worked_examples: Depthwise-separable replacement of the s4 layer (3x3, 64 -> 128, 56x56): depthwise 3*3*64 = 576 weights, pointwise 64*128 = 8,192, total 8,768 (8,960 with both biases) against 73,728 (73,856). MACs 8,768 x 3,136 = 27,496,448, i.e. 55.0 MFLOPs against 462.4. Ratio 73,728 / 8,768 = 8.41 = 1/(1/128 + 1/9).

GoogLeNet's inception (3a) 5x5 branch at 28x28 with 192 input channels and 32 outputs: direct 5*5*192*32 = 153,600 weights and 120.4 M MACs; with a 1x1 reduction to 16 channels first, 192*16 + 5*5*16*32 = 3,072 + 12,800 = 15,872 weights and 12.4 M MACs, 9.7x cheaper.

SmallResNet with every block convolution replaced by a depthwise-separable pair (Lab 3 extension): 187,018 parameters instead of 1,228,970, 6.6x fewer - less than 8x because the stem, the 1x1 shortcut projections, the batch norms and the head are unchanged and the first stage has only 32 channels.

figures.description: Standard versus depthwise-separable convolution as blocks: on the left one k x k x C_in filter per output channel (C_out of them); on the right C_in separate k x k x 1 filters producing C_in maps, then C_out 1 x 1 x C_in filters mixing them; each annotated with its MACs per position, k^2 C_in C_out versus k^2 C_in + C_in C_out.

The inception (3a) module: four parallel branches from a 28x28x192 input - 1x1 (64); 1x1 (96) -> 3x3 (128); 1x1 (16) -> 5x5 (32); 3x3 max pool -> 1x1 (32) - concatenated to 28x28x256, the 1x1 reductions highlighted, and the 5x5 branch's cost with and without reduction (120.4 M versus 12.4 M multiply-adds).

checks: Cost ratio of a depthwise-separable 3x3 to a standard 3x3 with C_in = C_out = 256? -> 1/256 + 1/9 = 0.115, about 8.7x cheaper.
A 1x1 convolution from 256 to 64 channels on a 14x14 map: parameters with bias, and MACs? -> 256*64 + 64 = 16,448; 16,384 x 196 = 3,211,264 MACs.

sections.title: The classic architectures: LeNet, AlexNet, VGG and Inception
sections.purpose: Read the first four landmark networks as a sequence of single ideas, each checkable with the counting tools of s3-s6.
must_cover: How to read an architecture table: per layer, output shape, kernel and stride, parameters and MACs, each confirmed with the formulas of s3-s4.

LeNet-5 (LeCun et al. 1998), the pattern conv -> subsample -> conv -> subsample -> dense (source): 32x32 input; C1 6@28x28 (5x5); S2 6@14x14 (2x2 subsampling with one trainable coefficient and bias per map); C3 16@10x10 with a partial connection table (each map sees 3, 4 or 6 of the S2 maps); S4 16@5x5; C5 120 (a 5x5 convolution on a 5x5 map, i.e. a dense layer); F6 84; 10 output units. It read bank cheques for a decade (source).

AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al. 2012): five convolutional and three dense layers, about 60 million parameters, trained on two GPUs (its grouped convolutions are that split); ReLU (their Figure 1: a four-layer CNN reached 25% training error on CIFAR-10 six times faster than with tanh); dropout 0.5 in the first two dense layers; augmentation with random 224x224 crops of 256x256 images, horizontal flips and PCA colour jitter; overlapping 3x3 max pooling. ILSVRC-2012 top-5 test error 15.3% against 26.2% for the next entry - state it this way rather than 'halved'.

VGG (Simonyan and Zisserman 2015): only 3x3 convolutions (stride 1, padding 1) and 2x2 max pools, channels 64 -> 512, 16-19 weight layers; the stacked-3x3 argument of s3; VGG-16 has 138 M parameters (89% in the dense layers) and about 15.5 G multiply-adds; simple, and still a common backbone and feature extractor (source).

Inception / GoogLeNet (Szegedy et al. 2015): parallel 1x1, 3x3 and 5x5 branches plus pooling, concatenated; 1x1 bottlenecks keep it cheap; 22 layers deep; the paper states it uses 12 times fewer parameters than AlexNet; winner of ILSVRC-2014 classification with 6.67% top-5 error; auxiliary classifiers on intermediate layers helped gradients reach early layers, a pre-ResNet fix for depth.

How the headline numbers are defined (Russakovsky et al. 2015): ILSVRC has 1.2 million training images in 1,000 classes, 50,000 validation and 100,000 test images; top-5 error counts a prediction correct when the true class is among the five highest scores; competition entries were often ensembles.
The thread: each network is its predecessor plus one idea, and error fell while parameters did not have to rise (VGG-16, 138 M; GoogLeNet, a few million).
worked_examples: LeNet-5 counted layer by layer: C1 6*(5*5*1 + 1) = 156; S2 6*2 = 12; C3 (6*3 + 9*4 + 1*6) = 60 kernel-input pairs x 25 + 16 biases = 1,516; S4 16*2 = 32; C5 120*(5*5*16 + 1) = 48,120; F6 84*(120 + 1) = 10,164; total 60,000 trainable parameters. Connections (multiply-adds): C1 28*28*156 = 122,304; S2 14*14*6*5 = 5,880; C3 10*10*1,516 = 151,600; S4 5*5*16*5 = 2,000; C5 48,120; F6 10,164; output 840; total 340,908, the figures LeCun et al. give. Weight sharing makes the connections 5.7 times the parameters.
A modern PyTorch 'LeNet-5' with full C3 connectivity and a linear 10-way output has 156 + 2,416 + 48,120 + 10,164 + 850 = 61,706 parameters, the number most tutorials print.

figures.description: Timeline 1998-2022, one box per network - LeNet-5, AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogLeNet, ResNet, DenseNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet, ViT, ConvNeXt - each with its one idea in three to five words and, where stated in the text, its parameter count; ViT marked with an arrow 'Module 06'.

Two stacked 3x3 layers against one 5x5, both 256 -> 256 channels, no bias: weights? -> 2 x 9 x 256^2 = 1,179,648 against 25 x 256^2 = 1,638,400.

sections.title: Residual networks
sections.purpose: Explain the degradation problem, the residual block and the gradient argument for why depth stopped being an obstacle, using the block every later architecture, the transformer included, reuses.
must_cover: The degradation problem (He et al. 2016, Figure 1): on CIFAR-10 a 56-layer plain network has higher training error than a 20-layer one, so the failure is optimisation, not overfitting. A deeper network could copy the shallower one and set its extra layers to the identity; the optimiser does not find that solution.

The residual block (source): h_{l+1} = h_l + F(h_l), with F two 3x3 convolution-BN(-ReLU) layers (basic block) or 1x1-3x3-1x1 (bottleneck); ReLU after the addition in the original design; a strided 1x1 projection on the shortcut when the shape changes (the source's skip). The block learns the change from its input.

Identity is easy (source): initialise the last layer of F near zero - in practice set the last batch norm's gamma to 0 (Goyal et al. 2017) - and the block starts as the identity, so a deep ResNet begins as a shallow network and grows into its depth.

The gradient argument written out (He et al. 2016b, identity mappings), for pre-activation blocks with nothing after the addition: summing h_{i+1} - h_i = F_i(h_i) gives h_L = h_l + sum_{i=l}^{L-1} F_i(h_i), hence dL/dh_l = dL/dh_L (I + d/dh_l sum_i F_i(h_i)). The identity term carries the top gradient to every layer unchanged (source: the gradient reaches early layers along a path of additions rather than a product of Jacobians); to vanish, the second term would have to cancel the identity exactly. Contrast the plain network's product of Jacobians (Module 02) and note that a ReLU after the addition gates the highway, which motivated the pre-activation form.

Scalar illustration: per-layer gain 0.9 over 50 layers gives 0.9^50 = 0.0052; gain 1.1 gives 117; a residual layer whose branch derivative is +0.01 or -0.01 gives 1.01^50 = 1.64 or 0.99^50 = 0.61 - near 1 without tuning.

Measured in Lab 3 on 8x8 digits (16-channel 3x3 layers): at initialisation without normalisation, the gradient reaching the stem of a plain network is 1.4e-5 at 9 layers, 9e-10 at 19 and underflows to 0 at 55, while the residual network's stays between 0.02 and 0.09; with batch norm the 55-layer plain network's stem gradient is about 190 (it explodes instead) against 0.8 with shortcuts. After 12 epochs the plain 55-layer network's training loss is still about 2.0 (chance is ln 10 = 2.30) while the residual one reaches 0.07; at 19 layers plain already trails (0.40 against 0.07).
The bottleneck block for deep ResNets (50, 101, 152 layers): 256 -> 1x1 -> 64 -> 3x3 -> 64 -> 1x1 -> 256.

Results (He et al. 2016): ResNet-152 on ImageNet; ILSVRC-2015 classification winner with 3.57% top-5 error (an ensemble); on CIFAR-10, 110 layers with 1.7 M parameters reach 6.43% error and 1,202 layers train but test worse (7.93%) - overfitting, not degradation. Depth stopped being an obstacle (source).

DenseNet briefly (Huang et al. 2017): every layer of a block receives the concatenation of all earlier layers' outputs and adds k new channels (growth rate; k = 32 in DenseNet-121, about 8 M parameters); strong accuracy per parameter, at the cost of activation memory for the concatenations. Concatenation (DenseNet, U-Net) keeps features separate and grows width; addition (ResNet) keeps width fixed.
The same form, x + F(x), wraps every attention and feed-forward sublayer of the transformer (source; Module 06).
Present the source's Block and SmallResNet code here, verbatim, with its arithmetic printed; its correct parameter count is 1,228,970.
worked_examples: SmallResNet counted (Lab 3): stem 928; blocks 18,560, 57,728, 230,144 and 919,040; head 2,570; total 1,228,970 parameters; 63,801,856 multiply-adds (127.6 MFLOPs) for one 32x32 image.
Bottleneck versus basic at 256 channels: 256*64 + 9*64*64 + 64*256 = 16,384 + 36,864 + 16,384 = 69,632 weights against 2 x 9 x 256 x 256 = 1,179,648, 17x fewer.

figures.description: The residual block: input h_l splits into the identity path (a straight line, or a strided 1x1 projection when shapes differ) and the branch conv3x3-BN-ReLU-conv3x3-BN, meeting at an addition followed by ReLU; a second panel shows the pre-activation variant (BN-ReLU-conv twice, nothing after the addition).

Degradation reproduced (Lab 3): training loss on a log axis against epoch for plain and residual networks with 7, 19 and 55 convolution layers on load_digits; plain-55 flat near 2.0, plain-19 above plain-7, the three residual curves together near 0.05-0.07.

Gradient flow along five blocks: the backward signal drawn twice, once through the residual branches (multiplied by each Jacobian) and once along the identity highway (unchanged), with dL/dh_l = dL/dh_L (I + ...) written underneath.

checks: A residual block with an identity shortcut has its last batch norm's gamma set to 0. What does the block compute at initialisation? -> ReLU(h) with the original post-addition ReLU, which is h for the non-negative inputs a previous ReLU produces: the identity.
Why is Figure 1 of the ResNet paper evidence of an optimisation problem rather than overfitting? -> The deeper plain network's training error is higher too, not only its test error.

sections.title: Efficient and modern CNNs, and where vision transformers fit
sections.purpose: Show how the post-ResNet designs trade accuracy against cost, how training recipes confound architecture comparisons, and where the vision transformer sits relative to CNNs.
must_cover: MobileNet (Howard et al. 2017): depthwise-separable blocks throughout (s6); a width multiplier alpha (channels x alpha, cost about x alpha^2) and a resolution multiplier rho (cost x rho^2); MobileNet-224 has 4.2 M parameters and 569 M multiply-adds at 70.6% ImageNet top-1. It runs on a phone (source).
MobileNetV2 (Sandler et al. 2018): the inverted residual - expand with a 1x1 (x6), depthwise 3x3, project with a linear 1x1 (no ReLU on the narrow output) - with the shortcut between the narrow ends.

EfficientNet (Tan and Le 2019), compound scaling (source: scale depth, width and resolution together by a fixed ratio): depth d = alpha^phi, width w = beta^phi, resolution r = gamma^phi, with FLOPs proportional to d w^2 r^2 because a convolution's cost scales with C_in C_out and H W; the constraint alpha beta^2 gamma^2 = 2 makes each unit of phi double the FLOPs; alpha = 1.2, beta = 1.1, gamma = 1.15 were found by grid search on the small B0. EfficientNet-B0: 5.3 M parameters, 0.39 B FLOPs (multiply-adds), 76.3% top-1 (Table 2 of the ICML paper; a later arXiv revision reports 77.1%, so quote the version you cite).

ConvNeXt (Liu et al. 2022; source: a ResNet modernised with the transformer era's training recipe, matching ViT): start from ResNet-50, first apply the modern recipe (AdamW, 300 epochs, mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, random erasing, stochastic depth, label smoothing), then change the architecture step by step. ImageNet-1k top-1 after each step, from the paper's Appendix C, Table 10 (ResNet-50 regime, rounded to 0.1; Figure 2 plots the same values): original recipe 76.1; modern recipe 78.8; stage ratio (3, 3, 9, 3) 79.4; 4x4 stride-4 'patchify' stem 79.5; depthwise convolution 78.3, then width 64 -> 96 80.5; inverted bottleneck 80.6; depthwise layer moved up 79.9, then 7x7 kernels 80.6; GELU 80.6; fewer activations 81.3; fewer normalisations 81.4; layer norm instead of batch norm 81.5; separate downsampling layers 82.0 (81.97 +/- 0.06). Table 1 reports the finished ConvNeXt-T at 82.1% (28.6 M parameters, printed as 29M; 4.5 G multiply-adds) against 81.3% for the Swin-T transformer (28 M, 4.5 G). Say which table each number comes from.
The lesson for reading papers: compare architectures only under the same training recipe; an improvement over a baseline trained with an older recipe may be mostly recipe.

The vision transformer, as a pointer only: two sentences and a link to Module 06, Section 8, which owns it, including the patch-embedding parameter count. ViT (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021; source: patches as tokens, no convolution, wins with enough data) cuts the image into 16x16 patches, embeds each as a token with what amounts to a 16x16 stride-16 convolution, and runs a transformer over them; with less built in than a CNN, it trails comparable ResNets trained on ImageNet-1k alone and matches or beats them after pretraining on far larger sets, Lab 2's inductive-bias lesson at scale.

A dated, conservative judgement (as of 2026): CNNs remain a default where data are scarce, inputs are large (high resolution, 3D), latency or power is constrained, or dense outputs are needed, and hybrids of convolution and attention are common.
worked_examples: EfficientNet's constraint: alpha beta^2 gamma^2 = 1.2 x 1.1^2 x 1.15^2 = 1.2 x 1.21 x 1.3225 = 1.92, about 2; at phi = 3 depth grows x1.73, width x1.33, resolution x1.52, and FLOPs about x1.92^3 = 7.1.

MobileNet's width multiplier alpha = 0.5: both C_in and C_out halve in the pointwise layers, which dominate the cost, so multiply-adds fall to about alpha^2 = 0.25 of the original (the depthwise part falls only to 0.5).

Recipe against architecture in ConvNeXt's numbers (Table 10): the recipe moves ResNet-50 from 76.1% to 78.8% (+2.7 points) and the architectural steps from 78.8% to 82.0% (+3.2). Compared naively with the 76.1% baseline, the published ConvNeXt-T (82.1%, Table 1) would credit the architecture with 6.0 points, 45% of which is recipe.

A paper reports a new architecture at 80.5% against a ResNet-50 baseline at 76.1%. What do you check first? -> Whether both used the same training recipe: the recipe alone moves ResNet-50 to 78.8%.

sections.title: Training a CNN: augmentation, normalisation and transfer learning
sections.purpose: Give the practical recipe for training a CNN on a small engineering dataset, with measurements that show when each ingredient helps and when it does not.
must_cover: Augmentation as the most effective regulariser for images (source), with the rule that every transform must leave the label true (source: a vertical flip of a digit is a different digit). Geometric: random crops (pad-and-crop, random-resized crop), flips, small rotations and scalings, elastic deformations (U-Net's key augmentation for microscopy); photometric: brightness, contrast, colour jitter, noise, blur. Rotations only where the label is rotation-invariant (source). For segmentation the mask receives the same geometric transform, with nearest-neighbour interpolation.

Mixing methods (source): mixup x~ = lambda x_i + (1 - lambda) x_j, y~ = lambda y_i + (1 - lambda) y_j with lambda ~ Beta(a, a), a around 0.2; CutMix pastes a rectangle of x_j into x_i and mixes the labels in proportion to area. Both make targets soft.

Augmentation must describe variation the deployment data contain. Lab 2's extension measures both sides: on centred 8x8 digits, +/-1-pixel shifts and +/-10 degree rotations lower validation accuracy from about 0.90 to about 0.83 at 20 images per class (the shifts are an eighth of the image, absent from the centred test set, and the 1,898-parameter network cannot absorb them); on the 16x16 canvas where digits really do move, re-placing each digit at a fresh random position every epoch raises test accuracy from 0.36 to 0.66 at 5 images per class and from 0.76 to 0.90 at 20.

Input normalisation (source): subtract the training set's per-channel mean and divide by its standard deviation; with a pretrained backbone use its statistics (source) - for torchvision's ImageNet models, RGB in [0, 1], mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406), standard deviation (0.229, 0.224, 0.225) - and also its channel order, value range and resize convention.

Batch normalisation in CNNs (source; Module 02 owns the mechanics): statistics per channel over (B, H, W); conv -> BN -> ReLU was ResNet's recipe; below about 16 examples per batch the statistics become unreliable and group norm (Wu and He 2018: per example, over groups of channels) or layer norm replace it. It is the number of independent examples, not the number of values, that matters. When fine-tuning with small batches, keep a pretrained backbone's BN layers in eval mode, and remember that requires_grad=False does not stop running statistics from updating in train mode.

Transfer learning (source): a backbone pretrained on a large generic dataset has learned edge, texture and shape detectors that transfer; replace the final layer with one for your labels and fine-tune - first the new layer at a normal learning rate, then the whole network at about a tenth of it (source's recipe). The options, in increasing order of data needed: keep early layers only; linear probe (frozen backbone); full fine-tuning; discriminative learning rates (smaller for earlier layers); training from scratch.

Which layers transfer (Yosinski et al. 2014: early layers general, later layers specific), measured in Lab 4 with a narrow source (digits 0-4, 675 images) and a target of digits 5-9: at 5 labelled images per class, scratch 0.90, keeping only the pretrained first block 0.92, a frozen backbone with a new linear head 0.65, the probe followed by fine-tuning everything at a tenth of the rate 0.83; at 20 per class, 0.95, 0.97, 0.78 and 0.96. A narrow source transfers only its early layers; ImageNet's 1.28 million images in 1,000 classes are why its whole backbone transfers (Lab 4 shows a torchvision ResNet-18 version as an extension that is not executed; no number here depends on it). The values are means over five seeds; at n = 20 every option but the linear probe lies within the seed-to-seed spread (0.01-0.03) of the others, so the argument rests on n = 5 and on the probe.

When pretraining helps less: He, Girshick and Dollar (2019) matched ImageNet-pretrained detectors trained from scratch on COCO given longer schedules; Raghu et al. (2019) found small accuracy gains from ImageNet pretraining on large medical-imaging datasets, with faster convergence. With a few hundred labelled images pretraining remains the default starting point, including for scientific images that look nothing like the pretraining set (source).

Small-data checklist: pretrained backbone or at least pretrained early layers; strong label-preserving augmentation; a small head; early stopping on a validation set split by specimen; results reported over several seeds and folds. Optimisers, schedules and the overfit-one-batch test are Module 02's; train with crops, flips where valid, and a cosine schedule (source).
worked_examples: Mixup with lambda = 0.7 between a 'cat' and a 'dog' image: the input is 0.7 x_cat + 0.3 x_dog pixel by pixel and the target (0.7, 0.3); the cross-entropy against this soft target is minimised by predicting exactly 0.7 and 0.3.

ImageNet normalisation: a white pixel (1, 1, 1) becomes ((1 - 0.485)/0.229, (1 - 0.456)/0.224, (1 - 0.406)/0.225) = (2.25, 2.43, 2.64) and a black one (-2.12, -2.04, -1.80). Skipping normalisation feeds 1.0 and 0.0 where the backbone expects these values; feeding 0-255 integers feeds 255. In Lab 4, feeding unnormalised pixels to the pretrained digit backbone drops the linear probe from about 0.72 to about 0.51 at 10 images per class.

Lab 4's transfer table (seeds 0-4; mean accuracy on the 224 held-out images of digits 5-9): n = 5 per class - scratch 0.898, first block kept and frozen 0.921, first two blocks frozen 0.899, linear probe 0.645, probe then fine-tune 0.826, first block then fine-tune 0.926; n = 20 - 0.954, 0.970, 0.967, 0.779, 0.963, 0.978.

sections.title: Detection: boxes, anchors, IoU and NMS
sections.purpose: Show how a CNN becomes an object detector, with the geometry, the losses and the post-processing written out, so that a detection paper's design choices can be read.
must_cover: The task (source: detection places boxes around objects): output a set of (box, class, score); boxes as corners (x1, y1, x2, y2) or centre and size (x, y, w, h).

Intersection over union: IoU = |A intersect B| / |A union B|, the intersection's corners being the larger of the two minima and the smaller of the two maxima. A detection is a true positive if its IoU with an unmatched ground-truth box of the same class is at least 0.5 (PASCAL VOC); COCO averages over IoU thresholds 0.50, 0.55, ..., 0.95.

Anchors: at each feature-map position, k reference boxes of several scales and aspect ratios (Faster R-CNN: 3 scales x 3 ratios = 9). For each anchor the network predicts class scores and offsets t = ((x - x_a)/w_a, (y - y_a)/h_a, ln(w/w_a), ln(h/h_a)); the logarithm keeps widths positive and makes scale errors relative. A feature map of about 60x40 positions gives about 2,400 x 9, roughly 20,000 anchors (Faster R-CNN's figure for a 1000x600 image).

The loss (source: classification plus box regression): a classification term over all anchors (cross-entropy or focal) plus a box term (smooth L1 on t, or an IoU-based loss) over anchors matched to objects.

Two-stage detectors (source: propose regions and classify them; Faster R-CNN): a region proposal network keeps a few hundred to a couple of thousand boxes, RoI pooling (RoI align in later versions) extracts a fixed-size feature map for each, and a second head classifies and refines. Accurate, slower.

One-stage detectors (source: predict boxes on a grid in one pass; YOLO, RetinaNet; also SSD): class and box at every cell or anchor in one pass; fast. YOLO v1's output is a 7x7 grid with 2 boxes of 5 numbers and 20 class probabilities per cell, 7x7x30. The roughly 20,000 mostly-background anchors swamp the loss; RetinaNet's focal loss FL(p_t) = -alpha_t (1 - p_t)^gamma ln p_t with gamma = 2 (alpha = 0.25 in the paper) silences easy examples.

Non-maximum suppression: sort by score; keep the highest; delete remaining boxes of the same class whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold (0.5 is common); repeat. It fails in crowds (true neighbours suppressed) and leaves duplicates if the threshold is too high; Soft-NMS decays scores instead of deleting.

Average precision: rank detections by score, compute precision and recall at each rank, AP = area under the interpolated precision-recall curve; mAP averages over classes (and, for COCO, over IoU thresholds).

DETR (Carion et al. 2020): a transformer predicts a fixed-size set of boxes, matched one-to-one to the ground truth by the Hungarian algorithm inside the loss; no anchors and no NMS (Module 06 explains the transformer). Instance segmentation as detection plus a mask head (Mask R-CNN) links to s12.
worked_examples: NMS at 0.5 on A (score 0.9), B (0.8), C = (20,20,30,30) (0.7) and D (0.6): keep A; delete B (0.681 > 0.5); keep C (IoU 0 with A); keep D (0.143 with A; B is already gone): A, C, D. At threshold 0.1, D also goes: A, C.
Anchor offsets: anchor centre (50, 50), 32x32; ground truth centre (54, 46), 40x24: t = (0.125, -0.125, ln 1.25 = 0.223, ln 0.75 = -0.288).

Focal loss with gamma = 2: an easy negative at p_t = 0.99 has cross-entropy 0.01005 and focal loss 1.0e-6 (factor 1e-4); p_t = 0.5: 0.693 against 0.173; a hard example at p_t = 0.1: 2.303 against 1.865 (factor 0.81).

Average precision: five detections ranked by score are TP, TP, FP, TP, FP against 4 ground-truth objects. Precision 1, 1, 0.667, 0.75, 0.6; recall 0.25, 0.5, 0.5, 0.75, 0.75. All-point interpolated AP = 0.25 x 1 + 0.25 x 1 + 0.25 x 0.75 = 0.6875; recall never reaches 1, so the last quarter contributes nothing.

figures.description: IoU geometry: two overlapping boxes with the intersection shaded and its corners labelled max(x1), max(y1), min(x2), min(y2); beneath, three box pairs at IoU 0.14, 0.50 and 0.68 to calibrate the eye.
Anchors and NMS: left, one feature-map cell with its 9 anchors (3 scales x 3 aspect ratios) drawn over an image; right, the A-D example before and after NMS at 0.5 with scores, B greyed out.

Pipelines as block diagrams: one-stage (backbone -> dense head with class and box per anchor -> NMS), two-stage (backbone -> region proposal network -> RoI pooling/align -> classification and box refinement -> NMS), and DETR (backbone -> transformer -> N box predictions -> Hungarian matching, training only).
Precision-recall curve for the five-detection example: the raw step curve, its interpolated envelope, and the shaded area 0.6875.

checks: Why predict ln(w/w_a) rather than w - w_a? -> It keeps the predicted width positive and makes errors relative: 10 pixels matter more on a 20-pixel box than on a 400-pixel one.

Two adjacent people produce true boxes with IoU 0.55. What does NMS at 0.5 do, and what are the options? -> It deletes the lower-scoring person; raise the threshold, use Soft-NMS, or use a set-prediction detector without NMS.

sections.title: Segmentation: FCN, transposed convolution, U-Net and Dice
sections.purpose: Show how a CNN labels every pixel, why U-Net's skip connections preserve boundaries, and how segmentation is trained and scored.
must_cover: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel (source); instance segmentation separates objects of the same class (Mask R-CNN). The output is a (C, H, W) map of logits and the basic loss is per-pixel cross-entropy averaged over pixels.

The fully convolutional network (Long et al. 2015; source: downsample then upsample): replace the dense head by 1x1 convolutions (a dense layer is a 1x1 convolution on a 1x1 map), so the classifier runs at every position; the output is coarse (stride 32) and is upsampled, with earlier, finer maps fused in.

Upsampling (source): interpolation followed by a convolution, or a transposed convolution, which scatters each input value through the kernel - the gradient of a strided convolution with respect to its input (s2), run forwards. Output size H_out = (H - 1)s - 2p + d(k - 1) + output_padding + 1. Checkerboard artefacts arise when k is not divisible by s because output positions receive unequal numbers of contributions (Odena et al. 2016); k = 2 or 4 with s = 2, or resize-then-convolve, avoid them (source: the former avoids the artefacts).

U-Net (Ronneberger et al. 2015; source): a contracting path (two 3x3 convolutions with ReLU, then 2x2 max pooling, channels doubling 64 -> 1,024) and an expanding path (2x2 up-convolution halving the channels, concatenation with the encoder map of the same resolution, two 3x3 convolutions), then a 1x1 convolution to class scores. The skip connections carry high-resolution detail the bottleneck has lost, so fine boundaries survive (source). The original used unpadded convolutions: 572x572 in, 388x388 out, with encoder maps cropped before concatenation; modern versions pad, so output equals input when the size is divisible by 2^depth.

Measured in Lab 5 (synthetic images; segment the circles, not the rectangles of the same brightness; Dice and IoU pooled over all validation pixels, so every pair quoted obeys D = 2J/(1 + J)): a tuned global threshold reaches Dice 0.64 (IoU 0.47) because it cannot tell shapes apart; in full mode the U-Net reaches Dice 0.966 and IoU 0.934, the same network without skips 0.953 and 0.909; the larger difference is near boundaries, where pixel accuracy within 2 pixels of the true edge is 0.950 with skips against 0.918 without.

Losses and metrics: Dice D = 2|P intersect G|/(|P| + |G|) = 2TP/(2TP + FP + FN); IoU (Jaccard) J = TP/(TP + FP + FN); D = 2J/(1 + J), so D >= J and both rank models identically. The soft Dice loss L = 1 - (2 sum p_i g_i + eps)/(sum p_i + sum g_i + eps) on probabilities (Milletari et al. 2016 square the denominator terms); its gradient dD/dp_i = (2 g_i (P + G) - 2I)/(P + G)^2 with I = sum p_i g_i, P = sum p_i, G = sum g_i; Dice plus cross-entropy is the common combination.

Imbalance: background dominates; an all-background prediction can score 99% pixel accuracy and Dice 0. Empty masks make Dice 0/0: the eps term, or computing Dice over the batch, defines it - state how empty images are scored.
U-Net is the standard architecture for biomedical segmentation (source); its output is a label mask, the input a meshing step expects (s13). The 3D U-Net follows in s13.
worked_examples: U-Net sizes with unpadded convolutions: 572 -> 570 -> 568, pool 284 -> 282 -> 280, pool 140 -> 138 -> 136, pool 68 -> 66 -> 64, pool 32 -> 30 -> 28; up 56 -> 52, up 104 -> 100, up 200 -> 196, up 392 -> 388. The first skip crops 568 to 392, 88 pixels from each side.

Transposed convolution sizes: H = 16, k = 4, s = 2, p = 1 gives 15*2 - 2 + 3 + 1 = 32; k = 3, s = 2, p = 1, output_padding = 1 gives 30 - 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 32. Contributions per output position along one axis, for an all-ones input and kernel: k = 3 gives 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, ... (uneven: a checkerboard in 2D); k = 4 gives 2 everywhere inside; k = 2 gives 1 everywhere.

Soft Dice on four pixels, p = (0.9, 0.8, 0.3, 0.1), g = (1, 1, 0, 0): I = 1.7, P = 2.1, G = 2, D = 3.4/4.1 = 0.829, loss 0.171; the gradient of D is +0.286 on each foreground pixel and -0.202 on each background pixel.
Imbalance: a 20x20 object in a 256x256 image is 400/65,536 = 0.61% of the pixels; predicting all background scores 99.4% pixel accuracy and Dice 0.

figures.description: U-Net in the style of the original: encoder blocks descending with map sizes (568, 280, 136, 64, 28 after their convolutions) and channels (64, 128, 256, 512, 1,024), decoder blocks ascending, grey copy-and-crop arrows for the skips, red arrows for 2x2 max pooling, green arrows for 2x2 up-convolution, a final 1x1 convolution to the class map.

Why skips matter, from Lab 5: one validation image, its ground-truth mask, the U-Net prediction and the no-skip prediction, errors coloured (false positives red, false negatives blue); the writer picks an image where the no-skip model's errors form a band along the object boundaries, as the boundary-band accuracies (0.950 against 0.918) predict.

Transposed convolution with k = 3, s = 2 in 1D: four input cells each scattering a 3-cell copy of the kernel into the output, with the overlap counts written beneath, and the resulting 2D checkerboard for an all-ones input.

checks: Dice is 0.9. What is the IoU? -> J = D/(2 - D) = 0.9/1.1 = 0.818.

A padded U-Net with four 2x2 poolings receives a 100x100 image. What goes wrong, and the fix? -> 100 -> 50 -> 25 -> 12 -> 6; upsampling gives 12 then 24, which cannot be concatenated with the 25x25 encoder map. Pad to a multiple of 16 (112) and crop the output.

sections.title: Signals and volumes: 1D and 3D convolution, and from masks to surfaces
sections.purpose: Carry convolution to signals and volumes, count what 3D costs, and follow an engineering pipeline from a microscopy or CT volume to a measured surface with its error budget.
must_cover: 1D convolution slides a kernel along a signal (source): sensor streams, the observation series of a digital twin, spectra. Causal convolution pads (k - 1)d on the left only, so the output at time t sees only inputs up to t (required for forecasting). The receptive-field arithmetic is the same (source).

Dilated causal stacks (source: WaveNet's design covers thousands of samples with few layers): kernel 2 with dilations 1, 2, 4, ..., 512 gives a receptive field of 1,024 in 10 layers. Temporal convolutional networks (Bai et al. 2018) are strong baselines against recurrent networks for sequence tasks (source: a serious competitor to recurrent networks for time series before transformers). Module 04, Exercise 15 (e15) replaces an LSTM forecaster with a dilated causal stack and compares the two.

3D convolution (source): a k x k x k kernel through a volume; parameters k^3 C_in C_out + C_out and MACs k^3 C_in C_out D_out H_out W_out, an extra factor of k over 2D. The 3D U-Net (Cicek et al. 2016) uses 3x3x3 convolutions and was trained from sparsely annotated slices.

Present the source's Down3D block (Conv3d - GroupNorm(8) - ReLU twice, then max_pool3d, returning the pre-pool map for the skip) and count it for 1 -> 32 channels: 896 + 64 + 27,680 + 64 = 28,704 parameters. Group norm because a volume batch is usually one or two stacks, where batch norm's statistics are meaningless (source).
Memory is the binding constraint in 3D (worked example): volumes are processed in patches (source) with batch 1-2, which is why group norm replaces batch norm.

Patch-based (sliding-window) inference: tile the volume with overlapping patches, predict, and blend the overlaps (average or Gaussian-weighted) to avoid seams; the U-Net paper's overlap-tile strategy is the 2D version.

Anisotropic voxels: confocal stacks are often 0.5 x 0.5 micrometres in plane and 2 micrometres between slices. Options: resample to isotropic, use anisotropic kernels (e.g. 1x3x3 in early layers), or per-slice 2D models. The spacing must travel with the data.

Cheaper 3D: the (2+1)D factorisation (a 1x3x3 spatial convolution followed by a 3x1x1 axial one) costs 9C^2 + 3C^2 = 12C^2 weights instead of 27C^2 at the same width; depthwise 3D convolutions as in s6.

From mask to surface (generalised from the source's image-to-mesh example): a U-Net trained on annotated microscopy or CT produces a voxel mask or probability volume; volume = voxel count x voxel volume; the surface is extracted as an isosurface by marching cubes (Lorensen and Cline 1987): visit each cube of 8 neighbouring voxel centres, classify the corners as inside or outside (2^8 = 256 cases, 15 up to rotation and complement), and place triangle vertices on cube edges by linear interpolation of the probability at level 0.5; mesh area and enclosed volume follow. Counting exposed voxel faces instead overestimates the area by a factor that does not shrink with resolution: 1.5 for a sphere (the faces add up to the projected areas on the three axis planes, twice each: 6 pi r^2 against 4 pi r^2), and 4/pi = 1.27 in 2D for a disc's perimeter (8r against 2 pi r).

The error budget for a measured volume, using Module 01's decomposition: bias from discretisation (the staircase), from the threshold level and from systematic segmentation errors; variance from noise and from where the object falls on the voxel grid; a gross error if the spacing is wrong. Evaluate segmentation models with splits by specimen (source failure mode).
worked_examples: WaveNet-style receptive field: kernel 2, dilations 1, 2, 4, ..., 512: r = 1 + sum (k - 1)d = 1 + 1,023 = 1,024 samples in 10 layers; three such blocks reach 3,070; undilated kernel-2 layers would need 1,023 layers.
3D against 2D parameters: a 3x3x3 convolution from 32 to 32 channels has 27*32*32 + 32 = 27,680 parameters against 9,248 for 3x3 in 2D.

Activation memory, float32, batch 1, a 128^3 patch, a four-level encoder with 32/64/128/256 channels and six stored tensors per level (two convolution outputs, two normalisation outputs, two activations): one 32-channel map is 128^3 x 32 x 4 B = 256 MiB; the levels hold 1,536 + 384 + 96 + 24 = 2,040 MiB, about 2.0 GiB, before the decoder, which costs about as much again. One 32-channel map of a 512x512 2D slice is 32 MiB.

Measurement on ideal shapes (NumPy and contourpy): a digital disc of radius 8 pixels has 201 pixels (pi x 64 = 201.1), a pixel-edge perimeter of 64 (= 8r, +27%), a marching-squares perimeter of 52.9 on the binary mask (+5%) and 50.2 on a slightly blurred mask (2 pi r = 50.3). A digital sphere of radius 10 voxels has 4,199 voxels (4,188.8 expected) and an exposed-face area of 1,884 against 4 pi r^2 = 1,256.6 (ratio 1.50; 1.51 at r = 5, 1.50 at r = 20).

On predicted masks (Lab 5, full mode, 221 isolated circles): area by pixel count averages 0.996 of pi r^2 (standard deviation 0.056); pixel-edge perimeter 1.27 times 2 pi r; the 0.5 iso-contour of the predicted probability 1.036 (standard deviation 0.041).

An anisotropic ellipsoid (semi-axes 12, 9, 7 micrometres; spacing 0.5 x 0.5 x 2.0; voxel volume 0.5 cubic micrometres): 6,372 voxels give 3,186.0 against 4/3 pi x 12 x 9 x 7 = 3,166.7 (+0.6%); over 20 random grid offsets the mean is 3,169.6 (bias +0.1%) and the standard deviation 29.5 (0.9%); the exposed-face area is 1,610 against the exact 1,083.1 square micrometres (+48.6%); marching cubes on the binary mask (scikit-image) still reports about 1,317 (+22%), because the 2-micrometre slices leave terraces in the mesh, against about 1,136 (+5%) after a 0.5-micrometre Gaussian blur, so mesh a probability volume or a lightly smoothed mask; the same mask read with spacing 1 x 1 x 1 reports 6,372, twice the truth. Exercise e14 repeats the analysis on a second ellipsoid at another spacing.

checks: How much left padding does a causal 1D convolution with k = 3 and d = 4 need to keep the output as long as the input? -> (k - 1)d = 8.

Why does the exposed-face area of a voxelised sphere not converge to 4 pi r^2 as voxels shrink? -> Every face is axis-aligned; the faces sum to twice the projected area on each axis plane, 6 pi r^2, at any resolution: refinement makes the staircase finer, not flatter.
Group norm with 16 groups on 64 channels of a 32^3 patch: how many values enter each mean? -> 4 channels x 32^3 = 131,072, all from one example.

sections.title: Looking inside: filters, saliency and Grad-CAM
sections.purpose: Give the cheap tools for checking what a CNN uses, derive Grad-CAM, and state what such maps can and cannot show.
must_cover: Early filters learn edges and colour blobs; later layers respond to textures, parts and objects (source; Krizhevsky et al. 2012, Figure 3; Zeiler and Fergus 2014). First-layer filters can be shown directly as small images; deeper filters cannot, so look at feature maps for a given input (source) or at the input patches that activate a unit most.
The saliency map (source; Simonyan et al. 2014): S_{ij} = max over colour channels of |dy^c/dx_{c,i,j}|, the gradient of the class score with respect to the input pixels; high-resolution but noisy.

Grad-CAM derived (Selvaraju et al. 2017; source: weights the last convolutional maps by their gradient): for class score y^c (before softmax) and the last convolutional maps A^k (k = 1..K, each with Z = H x W positions), alpha_k^c = (1/Z) sum_{ij} dy^c/dA^k_{ij} and L^c = ReLU(sum_k alpha_k^c A^k), upsampled to the input. The ReLU keeps regions whose features raise the class score.

Relation to CAM (Zhou et al. 2016), derived: with a global-average-pooling + linear head, y^c = sum_k w_k^c (1/Z) sum_{ij} A^k_{ij} + b^c, so dy^c/dA^k_{ij} = w_k^c/Z and alpha_k^c = w_k^c/Z: Grad-CAM equals CAM up to the constant 1/Z and the ReLU. Lab 6 confirms it to about 3e-10 (float32 round-off).
Resolution: the map is as coarse as the last convolutional layer (7x7 for ResNet-50 at 224x224; 16x16 for Lab 6's 32x32 inputs), so it says roughly where, not which pixels.

The use that matters (source): the sanity check that a classifier is looking at the object and not at a background it happened to co-occur with, the most common way an image classifier fails silently. Shortcut learning (Geirhos et al. 2020); a documented case: pneumonia classifiers on chest X-rays that partly identified the hospital system and generalised worse to other hospitals (Zech et al. 2018).

Lab 6's measured shortcut: when every training square carries a 3x3 bright corner marker, the model scores 1.00 on marker-correlated data, 0.68 on clean images and 0.64 when the marker is random; Grad-CAM puts 26% of its mass in the 6x6 corner (3.5% of the image) against 4% for a model trained on clean data; the saliency map's corner shares are 9% and 3%.

Caveats: (1) explanations can look plausible yet ignore the model - Adebayo et al. (2018) found some saliency methods barely change when the weights are randomised; run that test (Lab 6: Grad-CAM after re-initialising the last convolution and the head correlates 0.10 with the trained map, so it passes). (2) A map shows where evidence was found, not what feature or why. (3) A clean map on the images you looked at is not proof: use counterfactual tests (move or remove the object, change the background) and data from a different source.
worked_examples: The CAM identity with Lab 6's numbers: the head averages 16 x 16 = 256 positions, so alpha_k^c = w_k^c/256; the lab prints max |alpha - w/256| of about 3e-10.
Lab 6's shortcut numbers as stated above, used as the section's case study.

Grad-CAM on a ResNet-50 at 224x224 gives a 7x7 map. Can it tell which of two adjacent 10-pixel cracks the classifier used? -> No: each cell covers 32x32 input pixels; use an earlier layer, a saliency map or an occlusion test.

Section 10: 'Grad-CAM would have shown it in an afternoon'.
